question: We're playing best of five games to 11. In the third game, when do we switch ends?

answer.reasoning: The question asks when ends are changed during the third game of a best-of-five, 11-point match. Two rule sets bear on it. The standard Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 8.1.3, say players change ends 'in the third game when a side first scores 11 points' (except Handicap Matches), and ITTO 7.0 (5) Clause 5.6.10 describes the umpire calling 'interval, change ends' after the rally that first takes a side to 11 in a third game. However, the question's format — best of five games to 11 — matches the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0, format best-of-5-games-11, in force 2027-01-04, which differs: its Clause 8.1.3 changes ends only 'at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game', with the only mid-game change in that format being in the fifth game at 6 points (8.1.5). Per the instructions, the standard rule is given first, then the alternative format with its in-force date.
answer.answer: Under the standard Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) (in force 2025-04-26), Law 8.1.3: you change ends in the third game when a side first scores 11 points, except in Handicap Matches; the ITTO adds that the umpire calls the score followed immediately by 'interval, change ends' after the rally which first takes a side to 11 points in a third game. However, for the exact format you describe — best of five games to 11 — the Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0, format best-of-5-games-11 (in force 2027-01-04) apply, and they differ: in that format there is no change of ends during the third game itself; players change ends at the end of the third game only if there is to be a fourth game (Clause 8.1.3), and the only mid-game change of ends in that format is in the fifth game when a side first scores 6 points (Clause 8.1.5).

question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The question is whether an opponent shouting 'fault!' during your shot is a fault. Two sources bear directly: Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Law 13.4.5 makes it a fault if, in play, a player 'deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures', and Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) clause 5.9.1.4 states specifically that a player calling 'fault' to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke 'shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)'. ITTO 5.9.1.3 distinguishes shouting to one's own partner, which is not necessarily deliberate distraction — not applicable here since the shout was at the opponent. Law 7.3 gives the consequence: the side committing a fault loses the rally and the opposing side scores a point. Together these fully answer the question.
answer.answer: It is a fault by your opponent. Under Law 13.4.5 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, it is a fault if, in play, a player 'deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures'. The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.9.1.4, make this explicit: 'A player calling ‘fault’, etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)'. (By contrast, clause 5.9.1.3 notes that shouting to one's own partner who is about to hit the shuttle is not necessarily deliberate distraction — that exception does not apply to shouting at the opponent.) The consequence follows from Law 7.3 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2): 'A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a ‘fault’', and 'The side winning a rally shall add a point to its score' — so your side wins the rally and scores the point.

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question asks for every situation that counts as a let (a replayed rally). Law 14 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, is the dedicated 'LETS' section. Clause 14.1 says who calls a let, 14.2 lists all the let situations (14.2.1–14.2.7, with 14.2.3 expanded into 14.2.3.1 and 14.2.3.2), and 14.3 states the consequence (the rally is replayed by the last server). A Para Badminton exception (14.2.3.2.1, wheelchair) exists but is not mentioned because the question is not about para play. No Alternative Laws variant of Law 14 appeared in the sources, so the standard rule is given. Together these clauses fully answer the question.
answer.answer: A rally is replayed (a 'let') in the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 14. 'Let' is called by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire, to halt play (Law 14.1). It shall be a 'let' in every one of the following situations (Law 14.2): (1) the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4) — 14.2.1; (2) during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted — 14.2.2; (3) after the service is returned, the shuttle is caught on the net and remains suspended on its top — 14.2.3.1; (4) after the service is returned, after passing over the net the shuttle is caught in the net — 14.2.3.2; (5) during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle — 14.2.4; (6) in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach — 14.2.5; (7) a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision — 14.2.6; (8) any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred — 14.2.7. When a 'let' occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again (Law 14.3) — that is the replay.

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) how long play can stop for a bleeding injury, and (2) who may come on court to help. The sources cover both. For duration: Laws of Badminton Law 16.3.1 gives the umpire general power to suspend play; ITTO 5.14.2 gives the specific blood-injury rule (delay until bleeding stops/wound dressed); ITTO 3.6.1.4 says the Referee must resolve the situation 'well within a few minutes'; ITTO 5.14.1 says the Umpire times the delay and no treatment causing undue delay is allowed on court; ITTO 3.6.1.2 allows only quick relief (e.g., a bandage) on court, with time-consuming treatment only in regular intervals. For who comes on court: ITTO 5.14.1 (Referee decides whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required), ITTO 3.6.1.1 (Referee and Tournament Doctor go on court immediately when called), and ITTO 3.6.1.3 (maximum two persons on court to assist, with the same allowed to the opposing side). One assumption in the question needs correcting: the sources set no fixed number of minutes for the stoppage — the only time guidance is 'well within a few minutes' for the Referee to resolve the situation, plus the umpire's general power to suspend for as long as necessary.
answer.answer: How long you can stop: there is no fixed time limit in the rules. The umpire may suspend play 'for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary' (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.3.1). For a bleeding injury specifically, 'the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise' (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.14.2). The Referee must resolve the injury situation 'as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned' (ITTO Clause 3.6.1.4), and the Umpire times the delay (ITTO Clause 5.14.1). On court, only quick relief is allowed — the Tournament Doctor 'may apply a quick relief, such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals' (ITTO Clause 3.6.1.2), and 'no treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court' (ITTO Clause 5.14.1). Who can come on court: the Umpire calls the Referee onto court, and 'the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court' when called (ITTO Clause 3.6.1.1); 'the Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court' (ITTO Clause 5.14.1). Beyond that, 'the Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation', and 'in fairness, the Referee shall allow the opposing side the same consideration' (ITTO Clause 3.6.1.3). If play is suspended, the existing score stands and play resumes from that point (Laws of Badminton, Law 16.3.3).

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to a match and its score when water makes the court unplayable mid-game. The sources cover this directly: Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Law 16.3.1 allows the umpire to suspend play for circumstances not within the players' control, Law 16.3.3 states the score stands, and the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) clauses 5.11.2–5.11.5 give the procedure for a court that is temporarily not playable, the suspension call, and resumption. Together they fully answer the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: Play is suspended, and the score stands. Under Law 16.3.1 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), "When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary." Water dripping from the roof is such a circumstance: per Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), clause 5.11.2, "Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions," and clause 5.11.3 adds that if a court "is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play." The match is not restarted and no points are lost: Law 16.3.3 states, "If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point." Procedurally, when play is suspended the Umpire calls "Play is suspended" and notes "S" on the scoring device or score-sheet (ITTO 5.11.4); when play resumes, the Umpire notes the duration of the suspension, ensures the players are on the correct side and in the correct service courts, then calls "Are you ready?" followed by the score and "Play" (ITTO 5.11.5).

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question is about an opponent flicking sweat onto the court and what the umpire can do. The Instructions to Technical Officials contain a clause directly on point: itto-5.9.1.6 says a player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court shall be reminded the conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied if necessary. Law 16.7.1 (with 16.7.1.1–16.7.1.3) sets out the escalation the umpire administers for breaches of Law 16.6: warning, fault if previously warned, or fault for a flagrant offence; Law 16.7.2 adds that on faulting a side the umpire reports to the Referee, who may disqualify. The ITTO misconduct clauses (itto-5.17.3, itto-5.17.4) describe the on-court procedure (yellow card for a warning, red card for a fault, calling the Referee). Together these fully answer the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: Throwing sweat onto the court is specifically covered. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) (in force 2025-04-26), Clause 5.9.1.6: "A player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied, if necessary". So the umpire first reminds the player that the conduct is unacceptable. If it continues or is serious, the umpire administers a breach of Law 16.6 under Law 16.7.1 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26), which provides three steps: (1) "issuing a warning to the offending side" (Law 16.7.1.1) — done by calling "Come here" and "… [name of player], warning for misconduct" while raising a yellow card (ITTO Clause 5.17.3); (2) "faulting the offending side, if previously warned" (Law 16.7.1.2) — calling "… [name of player], fault for misconduct" with a red card, and the umpire must call the Referee on court and report immediately (ITTO Clause 5.17.4); or (3) "faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach" (Law 16.7.1.3). A fault for flagrant, repeated or persistent offences under Law 16 is itself a fault under Law 13.5. Finally, under Law 16.7.2, "On faulting a side (Law 16.7.1.2 or 16.7.1.3), the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match" — disqualification is signalled with a black card (ITTO Clause 5.17.5). In short: remind first, then warning (yellow card), then fault (red card) if repeated or flagrant, with the Referee able to disqualify.

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to a rally when the line judge could not see the shuttle's landing. The sources cover this directly: the ITTO line-judge instructions say how an unsighted line judge signals (itto-8.5, itto-8.8); the ITTO umpire instructions and Laws 17.6.6 say the umpire then makes the call (itto-5.8.3 with 5.8.3.1–5.8.3.3, itto-2.5, laws-17.6.6); and Law 14.2.6 plus itto-2.5 say that if neither the umpire nor the Instant Review System can decide, it is a 'let' (rally replayed), with IRS deciding the line call when in use. Together these fully answer the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: The line judge first signals that they were unsighted: "If unsighted, inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes" (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 8.5), and "UNSIGHTED" is one of the approved hand signals (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 8.8). The rally then continues under the Umpire's decision: "When another official is unsighted, the Umpire shall make the decision" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 2.5), and "Where there is no Line Judge or if a Line Judge is unsighted, the Umpire shall immediately call" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.8.3) — "Out" when the shuttle lands outside the line, or the score / "Service over" and then the score when the shuttle lands "in" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clauses 5.8.3.1 and 5.8.3.2). This matches Law 17.6.6 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, under which an umpire shall, "where an appointed official is unsighted, carry out that official's duties or play a 'let'". question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question asks whether a coach may stand at the side of the court during a match. The directly on-point source is ITTO clause 5.12.2 (Coaching from Off Court), which states coaches must be seated and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2). Law 16.2.1 and 16.2.2 define those intervals (60 seconds at 11 points in a game; 120 seconds between games). Supporting context: ITTO 5.12.1 and Law 16.5.1 restrict coaching while the shuttle is in play. Together these answer the question fully; no refusal needed.
answer.answer: No. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.12.2, "Coaches must be seated in their designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during the permitted intervals (Law 16.2)." The permitted intervals under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.2, are: not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points (Law 16.2.1), and not exceeding 120 seconds between the first and second game and between the second and third game (Law 16.2.2). So your coach may stand court-side only during those intervals; otherwise he must remain seated in his designated seat. Additionally, coaching itself is not allowed from the moment the players take up position to serve and receive, and while the shuttle is in play (ITTO 5.12.1; Law 16.5.1: "Only when the shuttle is not in play (Law 15), and until the players have taken up position to serve and receive shall a player be permitted to receive advice during a match.").

question: What weight range is allowed for a plastic shuttle, and since our hall gets really hot and stuffy in summer, can we use a special type made for hot weather?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) the allowed weight of a plastic (non-feathered/synthetic) shuttle, and (2) whether a special hot-weather shuttle type may be used. For (1), Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Law 2.2.6 gives the base shuttle weight of 4.74–5.50 g, and Law 2.3.3 (Non-Feathered Shuttle) applies that weight to synthetic shuttles while allowing up to 10% variation. For (2), Law 2.4 is the only clause addressing climate: it permits modifications to the specifications only with Member Association approval, where altitude or climate makes the standard shuttle unsuitable, and only if there is no variation in general design, speed and flight. No clause defines a special 'hot weather' shuttle type. The Instructions to Technical Officials add that the Referee is the sole judge of shuttle speed (ITTO 5.13.3) and that shuttles should be retested if temperature/humidity change substantially (ITTO 3.5.4.7). Together these answer both parts.
answer.answer:
Weight: A plastic shuttle is a 'Non-Feathered Shuttle' under Law 2.3. Its measurements and weight must be as in Laws 2.2.2, 2.2.3 and 2.2.6 — Law 2.2.6 sets the weight at 4.74 to 5.50 grams — but because synthetic materials differ in specific gravity from feathers, 'a variation of up to 10 per cent shall be acceptable' (Law 2.3.3, Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26). Applied to the 4.74–5.50 g range, that 10% tolerance works out to roughly 4.27 g to 6.05 g.

Hot weather: The Laws do not define any special 'hot weather' shuttle type, so you cannot simply use one on your own. The only provision is Law 2.4 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26): 'Subject to there being no variation in the general design, speed and flight of the shuttle, modifications in the above specifications may be made with the approval of the Member Association concerned, in places where atmospheric conditions due to either altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable.' So a climate-related modification is possible only with your Member Association's approval and only if design, speed and flight stay the same. In a match, the choice of shuttle speed is the Referee's decision alone (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.13.3: 'The Referee shall be the sole judge for deciding the speed of the shuttles to be used.'), and shuttles should be retested during the day if conditions change substantially, e.g. temperature and humidity (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 3.5.4.7).

question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: The question has three parts: (1) whether swearing is misconduct, (2) whether a yellow card given before 'Play' costs a point now, and (3) whether the card is recorded after the tournament. Sources found: Law 16.6.3 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26) makes offensive/inappropriate behaviour a breach; Law 16.7.1.1 provides that a breach is administered by issuing a warning to the offending side, and ITTO 5.17.3 (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26) shows the warning is the yellow card. ITTO 5.2.2.1 and 5.3.2 confirm the warm-up ends with the calling of 'Play', which indicates the start of the match, so the swearing happened before the match. ITTO 5.17.10 directly answers part 2: a card given before 'Play' has no effect on the score but is taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2, faulting if previously warned). ITTO 3.7.3 answers part 3: after the tournament the Referee reports yellow and red cards to BWF (or CC), which may trigger further sanctions. All parts are answered by the sources.
answer.answer: Swearing is misconduct: Law 16.6.3 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26) says a player shall not 'behave in an offensive or inappropriate manner', and Law 16.7.1.1 provides that the umpire administers such a breach by 'issuing a warning to the offending side' — the yellow card shown under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) (in force 2025-04-26), Clause 5.17.3. Because the warm-up ends with the calling of 'Play' (ITTO 5.2.2.1) and 'Play' indicates the start of the match (ITTO 5.3.2), the swearing occurred before the match. Under ITTO Clause 5.17.10, misconduct before the match on the Field of Play before 'Play' is treated as a warning/red card/black card, but 'Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match' — so it does NOT cost him a point now. However, the same clause says the card 'shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match (Law 16.7.1.2)', and Law 16.7.1.2 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2)) says the umpire shall fault the offending side 'if previously warned'. As for the record: yes — under ITTO Clause 3.7.3 (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26), 'The Referee shall immediately after the tournament send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions.' So the yellow card is reported after the tournament and may trigger further sanctions.
